title: Pakistan Launches Diplomatic Push to Uphold Islamabad Peace Deal as US-Iran Tensions Flare
excerpt: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire are testing Pakistan's dual role as mediator and military ally, with Islamabad scrambling to keep its diplomatic project alive.
body:
• Pakistan is intensifying diplomatic efforts to salvage the US-Iran ceasefire it helped broker, even as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed US strikes on Iran have shattered the truce.
  • Islamabad has told Iran at the "highest level" that attacks on Saudi Arabia are "attacks on Pakistan" — a sharp escalation in rhetoric from a country that has thousands of soldiers deployed in the kingdom.
  • China and Pakistan jointly called for a ceasefire during a meeting between Foreign Ministers Wang Yi and Ishaq Dar in Shanghai.
  • The UN Secretary-General has reiterated that "there is no military solution to this conflict" and called for stepped-up diplomacy.

Pakistan is mounting an urgent diplomatic offensive to salvage the crumbling US-Iran ceasefire it helped broker, even as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating American military operations against Iranian targets, and deepening fractures within Tehran's leadership threaten to pull Islamabad into the very conflict it has been trying to mediate.

Nuclear-armed Pakistan, which signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia last year and has thousands of soldiers deployed in the kingdom alongside a squadron of fighter jets, finds itself in an increasingly precarious position. The Houthis fired missiles at Saudi Arabia this week after accusing the kingdom of bombing an airport under their control, piercing a four-year truce in what has so far been a single but deeply alarming incident.

Red Lines Drawn

"Our top civil and military leaders have conveyed to Iran at the highest level that the attacks on Saudi Arabia are attacks on Pakistan," a Pakistani official told Reuters. "It is our red line."

The language marks a significant hardening of Islamabad's stance. While Pakistan had previously expressed anger at Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia earlier in the year, regional analysts say this week's Houthi escalation pushed frustration to a new level because Pakistani soldiers are deployed near the Saudi border with Yemen, increasing their direct exposure to any widening conflict.

"Pakistan wasn't anticipating that the tensions will rise so suddenly," said Muhammad Amir Rana, a Pakistani security analyst.

""We have invested a lot in it, and we have an interest in keeping it afloat."</p> <h2>What's Next</h2> <p>The next 30 days will be critical."

Ceasefire in Tatters

The US-Iran memorandum of understanding — which President Trump initially hailed as a diplomatic breakthrough — has collapsed into renewed hostilities. The US has carried out strikes on Iranian missile depots and air defences on eight consecutive nights, and two American service members were killed in Jordan on Friday, the first US fatalities since Trump declared the ceasefire "over" following Tehran's targeting of ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tehran has suspended its commitments under the MoU, claiming "the US violated its commitments." Meanwhile, Iran's chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf acknowledged in a television interview that "we must also use the tools of diplomacy" — even as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps appears to be dominating decision-making in Tehran, according to Pakistani officials.

"There is no military solution to this conflict," said UN Secretary-General António Guterres through his spokesman, calling for "stepped up diplomatic efforts towards a peaceful and durable settlement" that includes the full restoration of navigational rights around the Strait of Hormuz.

Pakistan's Double Role

Pakistan's frustration is rooted in the recognition that a Houthi-led escalation could be more destabilising than the Iranian missile strikes were. Disrupted shipping through the Red Sea — an artery Pakistan and many other countries depend on — could force intervention under the terms of its mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia.

China has thrown its weight behind Pakistan's mediation. Foreign Ministers Wang Yi and Ishaq Dar met in Shanghai this week and jointly called for a ceasefire and renewed dialogue between Washington and Tehran. Pakistan's Foreign Minister Dar had previously hosted crisis talks with his Turkish, Saudi, and Egyptian counterparts in Islamabad, after which he said both Iran and the US had "expressed their confidence in Pakistan to facilitate the talks."

But the escalation forced the postponement of an Iranian delegation's visit to Islamabad, according to two Pakistani officials. The delegation, led by Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni, arrived two days late, with discussions expected to cover the fate of the US-Iran deal.

What It Means for the Region

For the Gulf's large South Asian diaspora — including millions of Indians and Pakistanis working in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar — the escalation carries direct consequences. The conflict around the Strait of Hormuz has already disrupted oil and gas supply routes, with Pakistan imposing emergency measures including early business closures to stave off fuel shortages. A wider conflict could displace workers, disrupt remittance flows, and further inflate energy costs across South Asia.

"Yes, there is frustration, but that doesn't mean that we are abandoning this project," a Pakistani official said, referring to the mediation effort. "We have invested a lot in it, and we have an interest in keeping it afloat."

What's Next

The next 30 days will be critical. The US-Iran MoU was designed as a 60-day framework, and the halfway mark has passed with the ceasefire in tatters. Whether renewed military pressure creates leverage for diplomacy or ensures the negotiating window closes entirely remains the central question. Pakistan, for its part, is signalling that it will not abandon mediation — but that its patience has limits. "If Saudi calls us in, we will stand by them and there is no doubt about that," a Pakistani source told Reuters.
image_caption: Diplomats gather around a table for an agreement signing, reflecting the high-stakes negotiations Pakistan is undertaking between the US and Iran. Islamabad brokered an interim deal last month but escalating military strikes have put the ceasefire at risk.
nri_angle: The conflict directly affects the large Indian diaspora across the Gulf, particularly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, where shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz have already driven up fuel prices and threatened supply chains critical to South Asian economies.
